content.text: In regions such as Nigeria and Venezuela, where conventional [[LINK:https://coremerch.github.io/store/blog/payment-solutions-zimbabwean-[[LINK:https://coremerch.github.io/store/blog/digital-product-payment-solutions-west-africa-what-nobody|COREMERCH guide to digital]]-sellers-honest-side-side|Payment Solutions]] platforms like Stripe and PayPal are inaccessible, digital creators face significant challenges in [[LINK:https://coremerch.github.io/store/blog/setting-up-nowpayments-digital-store-everything-you-need-8|setting]] up online stores. Choosing the right infrastructure for a crypto store can make or break your digital business. This post examines two options from COREMERCH: Stack 01, using GitHub Pages and Apps Script, and Stack 02, utilizing Cloudflare Pages and Workers. Understanding the nuances between these stacks is critical for creators who demand reliability, speed, and ownership in their digital commerce solutions.
What Each Option Actually Offers

Stack 01 leverages GitHub Pages for hosting, which is free and straightforward for creators familiar with basic web development. It integrates Google Apps Script for backend logic, allowing for a quick deployment of up to three products. In contrast, Stack 02 offers a more robust solution with Cloudflare Pages, which provides enhanced performance and security features. This stack also uses Cloudflare Workers and Supabase for backend operations, enabling the deployment of up to five products. While Stack 01 can be up and running in just 4-6 hours using the Sovereign Blueprint, Stack 02’s deployment takes a full 48 hours but is end-to-end tested for reliability before handoff.
How They Handle Restricted Countries

Both stacks cater to creators in restricted countries by providing a reliable avenue for digital commerce without reliance on conventional payment platforms. Stack 01, while simple, may lack some advanced features beneficial for creators operating in high-risk environments. Stack 02, however, integrates stronger security measures and scalability options, making it a more resilient choice. This resilience is critical in unstable regions, where payment processing must be both swift and secure. The architecture of Stack 02 is built to withstand the pressures of financial isolation, giving creators peace of mind as they sell digital products.
Payment Speed, Fees, and Real Costs

Both stacks utilize NOWPayments for crypto payment processing, ensuring low fees of just 0.5%. However, the speed of payment confirmation can vary. Stack 01’s integration is quicker to deploy but may not be as robust under heavy traffic compared to Stack 02, which can handle larger volumes efficiently due to its optimized backend infrastructure. Both options are designed to facilitate instant payment verification, but Stack 02's architecture is built for scalability and efficiency, making it a better long-term investment for creators anticipating growth.
Ownership is paramount: after deployment, you control everything.
Ownership, Automation, and Delivery

One of the key differentiators of COREMERCH stacks is ownership. After deployment, creators own everything—no subscriptions or platform dependencies, which is critical in maintaining sovereignty. Stack 01 provides essential ownership features but with limited automation capabilities. Stack 02, however, not only allows full ownership but also incorporates more automated processes through its advanced infrastructure, ensuring that product delivery and order management are seamless. This level of automation reduces manual intervention, enabling creators to focus on their craft rather than technical hurdles.
Which Architecture to Choose Based on Your Situation

If you're a digital creator looking for a quick, straightforward setup and you have limited product offerings, Stack 01 could serve your immediate needs. Conversely, if you anticipate scaling your business and need a more resilient solution, Stack 02 is the clear choice. Its enhanced features and testing provide a solid foundation for growth and reliability. Ultimately, your choice should align with your business goals and the level of complexity you are prepared to manage as you build your digital storefront.

The difference between Stack 01 and Stack 02 is not which one works — both work — it is which one fits your situation. Stack 01 is the right choice if you want to deploy yourself, you are comfortable with Google Workspace tools, and your initial volume is under 100 orders per day. The Sovereign Blueprint at $47 documents the complete Stack 01 build with full source code and step-by-step configuration. Stack 02 is the right choice if you want the deployment done for you, you need higher volume capacity, or you want email deliverability infrastructure configured from day one. The Edge Commerce Stack at $197 has COREMERCH deploy Stack 02 under your accounts in 48 hours, end-to-end tested before handoff. Both are available at https://coremerch.github.io/products.html.
Stack 02 is built for scalability, designed to grow with your business.

The setup decision comes down to time versus depth. The Sovereign Blueprint at $47 gives you everything to build Stack 01 yourself in an afternoon or Stack 02 over a weekend — full source code, step-by-step configuration, and the NOWPayments integration guide. The Edge Commerce Stack at $197 has COREMERCH build Stack 02 for you in 48 hours, end-to-end tested before handoff, with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configured for email deliverability. Both paths lead to a store you own completely. Both are at https://coremerch.github.io/products.html.
Your Deployment Checklist

Read the Sovereign Blueprint before you start configuring anything — understanding the complete architecture before touching any settings prevents the most common configuration mistakes. Create all required accounts first: NOWPayments, Cloudflare or GitHub, Supabase or Google account, Resend or Gmail. Then configure the backend with all credentials before deploying it. Then deploy the backend and confirm the endpoint is live. Then configure NOWPayments with the endpoint URL. Then build and deploy the storefront. Then configure your custom domain if using one. Then run the mainnet test. Then check the order database. Then — and only then — share the URL. The sequence is not arbitrary. Each step depends on the previous one.
